story.patient: 84-year-old woman found on her kitchen floor on a cold night; admitted to the ward at 1:10 AM; ED ear temperature 35.0 °C (the device's lowest reading); a liter of room-temperature saline running; no active warming; on the heart monitor

timeline.beat: Heart rate 48. A hump right after every QRS (the Osborn wave, also called the J wave). Nurse thinks: 'Just shivering artifact.' MISTAKE 1 · KNOWLEDGE GAP: called the hump artifact
Ear temp 35.0 °C, its lowest reading. Nurse thinks: '35.0. She's warming up.' MISTAKE 2 · HABIT OVER STANDARD: trusted the ear, no core temp
Heart rate 42. She has stopped shivering and is confused. Nurse thinks: 'Stopped shivering. Finally warm.' MISTAKE 3 · ACTED TOO LATE: no recheck, no call

Real-time crisis: BP falls 98/58 to 76/42; heart rate 38; hard to wake; the humps grow. Core temperature (rectal, low-reading probe) 30.6 °C. RAPID RESPONSE: 'Room 8: core temp 30.6 °C, BP 76/42, hard to wake'

story.outcome: Moderate hypothermia, missed for 3 hours. The hump was the clue, not artifact.

memory_line: Cold heart: a hump after every QRS.
caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 2:30 AM. She's 84, found on her kitchen floor on a cold night.
• Heart rate 48. A hump right after every QRS (the spike of each beat)

❌ 3 mistakes, 3 error types
1️⃣ Knowledge gap: called the hump "shivering artifact"
2️⃣ Habit over standard: trusted the ear thermometer. 35.0 was its lowest reading. No core temperature
3️⃣ Acted too late: she stopped shivering and got confused. Called it "finally warm"
➡️ 4:10 AM: core temperature 30.6 °C, BP (blood pressure) 76/42, hard to wake. Rapid response.

❄️ Osborn wave (COLD HUMP)
• Also called the J wave: an extra hump where the QRS ends and the ST segment starts (the J point)
• A classic sign of hypothermia. It usually shows below about 32 °C and grows as the body gets colder
• Not only cold: it can also show with a high calcium or a brain injury. Look at the patient
• Other cold signs on the ECG (electrocardiogram): a slow rate, longer PR, QRS and QT
• Stopping shivering while confused means colder, not warmer

✅ The right move
• Hump after every QRS? Think cold
• Core temperature with a low-reading probe (rectal, per policy). Many ear and mouth thermometers can't read below 35 °C
• Warm her as ordered: heat to the trunk, warm blankets, a forced-air warmer, IV (intravenous) fluids warmed to 38 to 42 °C
• Keep her flat and move her gently: a cold heart is irritable
• Check her glucose and ask why she fell
• Confused, stopped shivering, slow heart, low BP? Call now. Rewarming, not atropine, usually fixes a cold slow heart

rn_checks: Osborn (J) wave: a positive hump at the J point (QRS end, ST start), usually below about 32 °C, larger as the temperature falls; also seen with high calcium and brain injury (Mattu 2002; Paal 2016; Maruyama 2004). OK?
Other hypothermia ECG signs in the caption only: slow heart rate, longer PR, QRS and QT, shivering artifact (Mattu 2002). OK?

Right move: core temperature with a low-reading probe (rectal on a ward, per policy; many ear and oral thermometers can't read below 35 °C); warm as ordered: heat to the trunk, blankets, forced-air warmer, IV fluids warmed to 38 to 42 °C; flat and gentle handling (irritable cold heart); check glucose, ask why she fell; stopped shivering plus confusion = colder, call now; cold bradycardia usually doesn't respond to atropine, rewarming treats it (WMS 2019; StatPearls; Paal 2016). OK?

Story numbers (softened after Vera's check): 84-year-old found on her floor, ED ear temp 35.0 °C (its lowest reading), no active warming, room-temperature saline; core 31.4 °C at 2:30 AM falling to 30.6 °C by 4:10 AM (moderate hypothermia); heart rate 48, 42, then 38; BP falling to 76/42 on a live counter; rectal core probe at the rapid response. Realistic?

30-day rule: ventricular fibrillation (off until Dec 22) is not shown or named; the caption only says a cold heart is irritable. Sinus bradycardia (Nov 22) appears only as a slow rate, not taught. OK?
